description: Human-curated finite pool of cross-domain ideas. Uniform sampling from this pool is not uniform sampling from all science or mathematics. Entries were written before the draw; no claim that any transfers to aliquot dynamics.

candidates.idea: Noether's theorem: continuous symmetries of a variational system give conservation laws; identifying the right symmetry can be more useful than following individual trajectories.
Renormalization: coarse-grain degrees of freedom and study the induced transformation of effective descriptions; fixed points and relevant perturbations organize behavior across scales.
Adiabatic invariants: in suitable slowly varying Hamiltonian systems, an action variable can remain approximately conserved despite substantial motion of the original coordinates.
Detailed balance: a reversible Markov process balances probability flux on each edge, enabling stationary measures and energy or entropy descriptions.
KAM theory: under quantitative nondegeneracy and smallness assumptions, many nonresonant invariant tori survive perturbation of an integrable Hamiltonian system; resonances identify failure modes.
Percolation: local connectivity rules can create or destroy infinite connected components; cluster exploration and cutsets separate finite connectivity from genuine infinite propagation.
Abelian sandpiles: local chip-firing operations commute in a suitable finite dissipative setting, and stabilization can be characterized through an odometer and a least-action principle.
Metastability and nucleation: long residence in an apparently stable phase can end through a critical localized fluctuation; residence time is not the same as permanent stability.
Stoichiometric invariants: left-nullspace vectors of a reaction matrix give conserved combinations of species; siphons and traps can constrain which species may disappear or persist.
Autocatalytic sets: a collection of reactions can collectively regenerate the catalysts and resources needed for its own continuation, even when no individual reaction is self-sustaining.

Epistasis in fitness landscapes: the effect of one component depends on the others, so individually favorable changes need not compose; accessible paths depend on interactions rather than marginal scores.
Synchronization: weakly coupled oscillators can phase-lock; a phase description can reveal collective organization that is obscured by amplitudes and individual trajectories.
Observability: distinguish internal states through their sequences of outputs; a proposed reduced state is inadequate if indistinguishable observations hide different future behavior.
Small-gain theorems: quantitative bounds on interconnected input-output gains can certify stability of a feedback system, provided the gain product and interconnection assumptions are controlled.
Electrical network methods: effective resistance, flows, and Dirichlet energy can characterize recurrence or transience of reversible random walks on locally finite networks.
Expander mixing: spectral gaps control how evenly edges connect vertex subsets and how quickly suitable walks lose initial-state information, subject to graph and measure assumptions.

Martingales and optional stopping: a conditional-drift quantity can constrain hitting behavior, but stopping-time and integrability hypotheses are essential; an expectation statement need not control every trajectory.

Large-deviation theory: rare sustained behavior can have a quantitatively different cost from typical fluctuations; rate functions describe exponential rarity when the required probabilistic structure is available.
Renewal-reward theory: analyze returns to regeneration points and sum the rewards of complete excursions rather than averaging individual steps; renewal assumptions must be justified.
Coupling: place different stochastic processes on one probability space to compare their trajectories, prove domination, or obtain convergence through coalescence.
Entropy compression: encode the history of a hypothetical indefinitely failing procedure too efficiently, deriving a counting contradiction when the encoding is reconstructible.

Error-correcting codes: redundant algebraic constraints and syndromes can detect or locate perturbations without retaining the entire original message; distinct errors must be distinguished by the checks.
Incompressibility arguments: most finite objects cannot have much shorter descriptions; a proposed universal structural description may be contradicted by counting description lengths.
Information bottleneck: seek a compressed representation that retains information relevant to predicting a target, rather than preserving every detail of the original state.

Symbolic dynamics: encode trajectories as symbol sequences and describe admissibility through forbidden words or transition constraints; a symbolic itinerary need not be realized by an original-system orbit.

Finite-automaton pumping: a sufficiently long accepted path repeats a state and yields a pumpable segment; transferring this to an infinite-state system requires an exact, not merely suggestive, finite abstraction.
Well-quasi-orders: every infinite sequence has a comparable pair in the forward direction; Dickson's lemma applies to fixed-dimensional nonnegative integer vectors under componentwise order.

Size-change termination: track strict and weak descent of well-founded quantities across transitions; suitable composed transition graphs force an infinite descending thread in any hypothetical infinite execution.

Abstract interpretation: a sound over-approximation transfers invariants from a simpler state space to a concrete program; abstraction refinement removes spurious behaviors introduced by information loss.
Konig's infinity lemma: an infinite, finitely branching rooted tree has an infinite branch; arbitrarily long finite objects do not suffice without the branching and compatibility hypotheses.

Garden-of-Eden theorems: for cellular automata over suitable groups, locality and translation invariance relate surjectivity to pre-injectivity; forbidden predecessors and information loss are dual under precise hypotheses.
Graph separators and treewidth: a global constraint problem can become tractable when its interaction graph can be split through small boundaries whose states summarize communication between pieces.

Poincare recurrence: a measure-preserving transformation on a finite-measure space returns almost every point to neighborhoods of its starting point; finite measure and almost-everywhere scope are indispensable.
Optimal transport: compare distributions by the least cost of moving mass; a geometry adapted to the cost can expose contraction or a gradient-flow structure invisible in ordinary coordinates.
Persistent homology: track which topological features survive as a filtration scale changes, distinguishing robust multi-scale structure from short-lived features.
Discrete curvature and Gauss-Bonnet: local combinatorial curvature contributions can sum to a global topological constraint; the local-to-global identity is the essential mechanism.

Tropicalization and valuations: replace multiplicative structure by additive valuation data and study piecewise-linear shadows; cancellation where valuations tie contains information lost by the shadow.

Local-global principles and their failures: compatibility modulo prime powers or over completions may be necessary yet insufficient for a global integer solution; identify the obstruction rather than equating local consistency with existence.

Generating functions and singularity analysis: encode a family of discrete objects in a function and infer counting asymptotics from its analytic singularities when the combinatorial encoding and analytic hypotheses are established.

Projective metric contraction: suitable positive linear operators contract ratios in a cone, separating scale growth from convergence of shape; positivity and finite projective diameter are substantive assumptions.
